title: Where the lost kings went
hookLine: the third challenger brings a question he got from a spirit, and Yajnavalkya answers with the wind: each single thing, and everything together
carry: your breath is the world's breath
tomorrow: if the self is real, why can't anyone point to it?
last: KARMA: YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DO.

lines: A SPIRIT IN A STUDENT'S STORY.
IT KNEW THE ENDS OF THE WORLD.
cards: The third challenger opens with a ghost story. When I was a student, says Bhujyu, we wandered to a house in the land of the Madras. The householder's daughter was possessed by a spirit, a gandharva.
We asked it who it was, and it told us its name. Then we asked it about the ends of the world, and where the Parikshitas went. So, Yajnavalkya, I'm asking you: where did the Parikshitas go?
It's a trap with the answer already in his pocket. He heard it from a spirit. Let's see if this man knows it too.

teach.b: Who were the Parikshitas? The family of King Parikshit, remembered as great performers of the horse sacrifice, the one that opened this Upanishad two weeks ago.
The Mahabharata tells of a Parikshit too, Arjuna's grandson; the Upanishad doesn't explain, it assumes its listeners know. Yajnavalkya answers without a pause.
The spirit told you, surely, they went where those who perform the horse sacrifice go. And where is that? Then he gives a map.
This world is as wide as thirty-two days of the sun's chariot. The earth surrounds it, twice as wide. The ocean surrounds the earth, twice as wide again.

teach.h: A GAP THIN AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.
teach.b: And between them is a gap as thin as the edge of a razor, or the wing of a fly. Through that gap, Indra, as a bird, handed the Parikshitas to the wind, and the wind carried them on.

teach.h: WIND: EACH THING, AND ALL TOGETHER.
teach.b: Then the key line: so wind is each single thing, and wind is everything together. Whoever knows this escapes dying again. And Bhujyu falls silent.
Here's the teaching under the riddle.
Across this Upanishad, breath in the body and wind in the world are paired as one power, and Hindus call the life-breath prana. Twelve days ago, breath was the one singer the demons couldn't pierce.
Here, at the scale of the universe, it carries a person beyond the world.

teach.h: YOUR BREATH IS THE WORLD'S BREATH.
teach.b: That's why breath sits near the heart of Hindu practice, from pranayama to a mantra said on the out-breath: the most personal thing you have is also the thing you share with everything.

how: Vayu, the wind, is honored in Hindu tradition as a deity and as the cosmic breath, and breath, prana, is at the center of practices like pranayama; Yajnavalkya's answer to Bhujyu is read as praise of wind as both the individual and the whole.

o: wind, the great breath of the cosmos
the ocean that circles the whole earth
the sun's chariot that crosses the sky

games.q: what's inside the answer — tap the pairs.
p: thin as a razor's edge or a fly's wing
each single thing, and all together

s: Bhujyu learned his question from a spirit
a gandharva possessing a householder's daughter, he says.
Yajnavalkya says the way out of the world is a wide gate
a gap as thin as a razor's edge or the wing of a fly.
the Upanishad explains who King Parikshit was
it assumes its listeners know. the Mahabharata names a Parikshit as Arjuna's grandson.

games.q: Bhujyu thinks he's asking about a lost royal family. what is Yajnavalkya's answer really about?
o: wind, the breath that is each single thing and all things together.
a map for finding where the old kings are buried.
the gandharva spirit, who rules over the dead.
games.why: the wind carries the Parikshitas through, and wind is each single thing and everything together. knowing this, the text says, one escapes dying again.

practice: Hindus call this prana. Notice the tiny gap at the top of each in-breath, before the out-breath begins, thinner than a fly's wing; don't hold it, just notice it each time.
Then notice that the air moving through you is the same air moving through the trees outside, and the city, and the sea. Each breath yours; all breath shared.

wordCard.voice: Vayu, wind. Yajnavalkya's answer: through a gap as thin as a razor's edge, carried by vayu, each single thing and everything together.

orig.note: Sanskrit vāyu: wind, from vā, to blow. in this answer, both each single thing (vyaṣṭi) and all together (samaṣṭi).

carryVoice: Take this with you: your breath is the world's breath. Tomorrow, a practical man who wants to be shown. Until then.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Parikshit, grandson of Arjuna)
